draft.title: Extracting resources
card: Extracting a resource means taking it from the Earth. Mining digs out coal, metal ores and sand. Drilling reaches oil and gas deep underground.
Extraction can bring jobs and income to a region. It supplies energy for homes and transport, and materials for buildings, phones and machines.
Extraction can damage land when it is cleared or dug up. It can pollute rivers and groundwater, and destroy habitats where plants and animals live.
Because there are both benefits and risks, people weigh one against the other. Companies and governments often plan ways to reduce harm, such as repairing the land after mining ends.
draft.remember: Extraction gives us jobs, energy and materials, but it can harm land, water and habitats, so people weigh both sides.

a.q: Which of these is a risk of mining a resource?
opts: Waste from the mine may pollute a nearby river
The mine may create jobs for people in the region
The mine may supply metal for making machines
The mine may provide energy for nearby towns
a.why: Pollution of water is a way extraction can harm the environment. The other options are benefits: jobs, materials and energy.
a.clue: Which option is harm rather than a gain?

b.q: A company wants to open a coal mine near a farming town. The mine would employ 300 people but could harm local rivers. What should the council do?
opts: Weigh the new jobs against the possible harm to the rivers
Approve it, because jobs always matter more than rivers
Reject it, because every mine must damage the environment
Approve it, because coal is a renewable resource
b.why: Extraction has both benefits and risks, so a decision should weigh them. Saying jobs always win or that harm is certain ignores one side. Coal is not renewable, and that is not a reason to approve it.
b.clue: The card says people weigh benefits against risks.

a.best: Waste from the mine may pollute a nearby river

b.best: Weigh the new jobs against the possible harm to the rivers

problems.detail: The clue ('The card says people weigh benefits against risks') uses the same word as the right option ('Weigh the new jobs…'), so it gives the answer away.

The right option stands out. It is the only one not in the form 'Approve/Reject it, because…', and the other three are easy to rule out because they use 'always' or 'must' or state a plain falsehood. A student could pick it without knowing the idea.
